rows.message:
Harden the expression engine with real-world edge-case tests (#13)

Closes remaining gaps in expression fidelity before relying on it more
heavily, per the issue - breadth from real-world usage, not a rewrite
of the core grammar.

Sourced real coverage rather than inventing plausible-looking cases:
- GitHub's own documented object-filter (`.*`) examples (fruits.*.name,
  and the vegetables.*.ediblePortions example that's explicit the
  result is an array of arrays, not flattened).
- GitHub's own documented type-coercion table for cross-type `==`/`!=`
  and relational comparisons.
- Expressions pulled from real, currently-running public workflows:
  actions/checkout's `runner.os` comparisons, and git/git's CI
  (concurrency-group fallback via `||`, an empty-vars-means-all-
  branches `== '' || contains(...)` pattern, and a ternary-via-short-
  circuit idiom built entirely out of `&&`/`||`).

That survey found a real bug, not just a coverage gap: hyphenated
job/step ids - kebab-case is the dominant real-world convention
(`needs.ci-config`, `matrix.node-version`) and git/git's own CI relies
on exactly this pattern - previously threw a syntax error. The lexer's
identifier characters didn't include `-`, even though GitHub's own
property-dereference grammar does, specifically to accommodate
kebab-case ids without forcing bracket syntax everywhere. Fixed by
widening the identifier character class; a leading `-` stays excluded
(matching GitHub's own id-naming rule), so a bare `-` this engine has
no subtraction operator for remains an unambiguous syntax error.

One divergence was found and deliberately left open rather than fixed:
numeric-string coercion uses JavaScript's `Number()`, where GitHub's
docs specify a string is "parsed from any legal JSON number format,
otherwise NaN" - stricter than `Number()` (no hex, no leading `+`, no
leading zeros ahead of a nonzero digit). `'0x10' == 16`, `'+5' == 5`,
and `'007' == 7` all evaluate `true` here where a real runner would
get `false`. Real workflows essentially never compare against a hex or
leading-zero string, and rewriting the coercion grammar is a bigger,
more deliberate change than this pass's scope - documented in the
README's new "Confirmed expression-engine divergences" section and
locked in by a test, so it can't silently drift further without the
diff being visible.

Also added: multi-hop filter chains (github.event.commits.*.author.
email), deeply nested fromJSON indexing, mixed-type comparisons
(null/''/array/object cross-type coercion, same-instance-only object
equality), and the documented format() escaped-brace example.

252 tests passing (226 existing + 26 new), tsc --noEmit and next build
both clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Add time-travel: browse any executed step without disturbing the live pointer (#17)

Shipped as the "cheap version" the issue's own notes anticipated - the
stepIndex-aware /api/sessions/[id]/context endpoint and StepRunRecord's
per-step data already reconstruct history on demand, so this is UI on
top of an engine that already had what it needed, not an engine change.

New pure module (timeTravel.ts, unit-tested independently of React,
matching the keyboardShortcuts.ts precedent from #5):
- liveStepIndex(lane): the step index the debugger cursor sits on - the
  next step to run, or the last one once the lane's finished. Hoisted
  out of the three call sites in DebuggerApp that already computed this
  ad hoc, so the definition can't drift.
- isLiveSelection(session, selection): true only for the active lane at
  its live step index. A different lane, or an earlier step in the
  active lane, is always "history" - precise enough that it can never
  be confused with what Step/Continue/Run actually act on, which is
  always activeLaneId and unaffected by browsing.
- clampToHistory/canGoBack/canGoForward: the navigable range is a
  lane's first step up to (and including) its live cursor - never past
  it, since there's nothing to show for a step that hasn't run yet.
- liveSelection(session): where "Jump to live" goes.

New TimeTravelBar component, rendered above the step detail panel:
a LIVE/HISTORY badge, Prev/Next buttons to scrub through a lane's
already-executed steps, and a "Jump to live" button shown only when
viewing history. Reuses the same onSelect callback WorkflowGraph
already had for clicking a step directly - no new state in DebuggerApp,
just a second way to move the same selection.

Works across matrix lanes without special-casing: the bar operates on
whichever lane `selection` currently points at (falling back to the
active lane), so switching lanes via the existing Matrix tab or a
multi-lane failure jump (e.g. "Run all" failing a lane that isn't
active) is already exactly the "different lane, so it's history" case
isLiveSelection is built to recognize.

20 new tests (15 pure-logic, 5 component) plus a live-browser pass:
stepped through a 3-step workflow, confirmed the live badge/step
label/next-disabled state, browsed back via Previous (history badge,
previous-disabled at step 1, context inspector correctly refetching
for the historical step), and confirmed Jump to live returns to the
exact prior live state. 272 tests passing, tsc --noEmit and next build
both clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Visual polish: accessible status colors, a real running indicator, dagre graph layout (#11)

Status colors, consistency across surfaces:

A single statusStyles.ts module now defines every status's color, a
redundant non-color glyph (WCAG 1.4.1 - color is never the only signal),
and whether it renders as a hollow ring (hasn't run yet) or a filled dot
(has). It replaces three independently hand-copied color maps in
JobNode, MatrixExplorer, and StepDetailPanel that had already quietly
drifted apart:

- "pending" alone had three different treatments: JobNode used
  `#484f58` (contrast-checked at ~2.2:1 against every panel background
  in this theme - below even the 3:1 WCAG non-text minimum, so the dot
  was nearly invisible), MatrixExplorer fell through to a generic
  gray-700/gray-400 badge for anything it didn't recognize, and
  StepDetailPanel used a bare `text-gray-500`. Now all three use one
  shared, accessible value (#9aa4b2, ~7:1 against every background).
- "pending" and "skipped" - both grayscale, easy to mistake for each
  other at a glance - are now told apart by shape too: pending renders
  as a hollow ring (nothing has happened yet), skipped as a filled dot.
- MatrixExplorer's badge and StepDetailPanel's status word now show the
  same glyph as the graph's dot (✓/✕/–/▶/⊘), not just matching text.

Currently-executing indicator, actually observable this time:

The old `animate-pulse` was applied to a `lane.status === "running"`
value that - in this synchronous request/response engine - is set and
cleared entirely server-side within one HTTP round trip. The client
never actually receives a "running" SessionView; that class was dead
code from the browser's perspective. Replaced with a real client-driven
signal: `busy` (already tracked in DebuggerApp) threads through
WorkflowGraph into JobNode, and whichever step is the lane's live
pointer gets an animated spinning ring while a control request is in
flight - the only place "this is happening right now" is ever actually
true from the browser's point of view.

Graph layout:

Replaced the fixed `x: level * 340, y: index * 280` grid - which didn't
account for node height (a matrix job's lane selector, more or fewer
steps) and just got worse as a workflow grew - with `@dagrejs/dagre`'s
layered (Sugiyama-style) algorithm. Each node's height is estimated
from its own content before layout runs, and only jobs reachable from
`session.graph.levels` go through it (dagre needs a DAG; a `needs`
cycle is still placed separately, as before).

Verified against a new 12-job example workflow (`06-large-graph.yml`) -
one fan-out into five parallel jobs (including a 3-combo matrix job),
converging through two more levels back into a single job - covering
the "many jobs/levels" and "uneven fan-out/fan-in" cases the old grid
handled worst. A Playwright pass confirms all 12 render with zero
overlapping boxes (checked programmatically via bounding rects, not
just by eye), and a live run with a mocked failure showed the full
color/glyph system - success/failure/skipped all visually distinct and
consistent between the graph and the step detail panel - working
together with the existing time-travel bar and mock-outputs editor
without regression.

29 new tests (statusStyles, StatusDot, graphLayout, JobNode's
executing-indicator behavior) plus the Playwright verification above.
296 tests passing, tsc --noEmit, eslint, and next build all clean.

Add light theme + tablet-width responsive layout (#12)

Every hardcoded color (bg-*, text-white, text-gray-N, border-gray-N,
bg-gray-N) becomes a CSS-custom-property-backed Tailwind token (bg,
status, ink), letting a [data-theme="light"] selector in globals.css
override the whole palette at once. Dark's token values were chosen to
be byte-identical to the app's existing rendered colors, so dark mode
is unchanged.

A toggle in the top bar (src/components/ThemeToggle.tsx) flips
data-theme and persists the choice to localStorage via a new
src/lib/theme.ts module. An inline script injected in layout.tsx's
<head> applies a stored preference before hydration, so a returning
light-mode visitor never sees a dark flash.

The 6 buttons with a solid color fill (bg-status-running/failure) keep
literal text-white in both themes on purpose - white-on-blue doesn't
need to invert with the app theme.

Layout: the graph/right-panel row in DebuggerApp and the step detail
panel's two-column grid now stack vertically below the lg breakpoint
instead of clipping a fixed-width panel against a squeezed graph,
verified live at 820px width in both themes.

Add matrix lane search/filter and "debug this combination only" (#10)

A search/filter box now appears above the lane list once a matrix's
combinations exceed a threshold (>8 in the job node's dropdown, >6
across the Matrix tab) - small matrices stay unfiltered so it's not
one more thing to click past for 2-3 combos.

"Debug this combination only" is a new 🎯 toggle on every lane row (job
node and Matrix tab alike). Toggling it makes that lane the steppable
one and marks it "focused" - purely client-side view state
(focusedLaneId in DebuggerApp, new src/components/focusLane.ts for the
display label), never sent to the engine. While a lane is focused,
every sibling combination across every matrix job dims in the Matrix
tab, and the focus is visible from three places at once so it's
unambiguous without opening a tab to check: an amber "FOCUSED" tag +
border on the job node, a "Focused: <job> - <combo>" banner with a
one-click "Show all combinations" in the Matrix tab, and a dismissible
pill in the top bar.

Verified live with a 12-combination matrix (4 node versions x 3 OSes)
in both light and dark themes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Show intermediate evaluation steps in the expression playground (#9)

Builds directly on the existing lexer/parser/evaluator, as the issue's
notes anticipated - no changes to evaluation logic itself.

src/lib/expressions/trace.ts mirrors evaluator.ts's node dispatch to
build a full sub-expression tree instead of just a final value, kept
as a genuinely separate module (not a modified evalNode) so the
production evaluator that the real engine's if:/output resolution
depends on is untouched. A 41-fixture agreement test cross-checks
every traced result against the real evaluateExpression for the same
input, to catch any future divergence between the two immediately -
the lesson from #11's three drifted status-color maps, this time with
a test.

Every sub-expression shows its own value, in evaluation order.
matrix.node/steps.*.outputs.result-style chains are tagged with the
context path they resolve to. A ==/!=/relational comparison whose
operand types differ gets a coercion note. The untaken side of &&/||
is shown as "not evaluated - short-circuited" rather than inventing a
result for code GitHub's real short-circuit semantics never run. A
failure inside a nested call (contains(fromJSON(badJson), x)) is
flagged exactly at the fromJSON(...) node that caused it, with only a
lightweight bubbled marker on ancestors - not a generic
whole-expression error. A syntax error gets a caret under the exact
character position instead.

The trace is masked through the same maskObjectStrings as the plain
result, since a node can itself be secrets.TOKEN.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Add shareable session links (#8)

No server-side storage: a link is a self-contained, URL-safe base64
token (src/lib/share.ts) holding the workflow YAML, breakpoints,
What-If env/var overrides, mocked step outputs, and per-lane execution
progress.

The server discards the raw workflow YAML once it's parsed, so it's
cached client-side by content hash (workflowSourceCache.ts, the same
key SessionView.workflowHash already exposes) the moment a session is
created - the one place the app ever sees that text - and read back
when "Share" is clicked in the top bar.

Opening a link (/share/[token]) creates a brand-new session from that
YAML, then replays it into the shared state by calling the same
control/breakpoint/What-If/mock APIs a real user would - not by
injecting server state directly. Reconstructing "pointer position" for
a multi-job workflow turned out to be the real work: a downstream
job's lane stays blocked until its needs all reach a terminal status,
exactly like normal execution, so replay tracks every lane that had
progressed (not just the one being viewed) and retries whichever
aren't blocked each pass, until the shared state is reached.

Secrets are never included in a share link - not values, not even
names, stricter than debugPrefs' local-only persistence, since a link
can leave the browser entirely. A dismissible "Viewing a shared
session" banner (?shared=1) makes the distinction from an own session
unambiguous, and the Share button explains itself rather than failing
silently when the workflow text isn't cached in the current browser.

Verified live against the needs-chain example workflow (lint -> test
-> deploy/notify, test failing on purpose): the reconstructed
session's lane statuses, pointers, and breakpoint all matched the
original exactly, confirmed via direct session-state comparison in
both a fresh browser context and both themes.

Add a one-click failed-step example to the home page

A prominent button next to the header creates a session from a small

Mocking the failure instead of trusting real execution matters

default and are never actually executed. A demo button that relied on
its own exit 1 would silently show nothing failing on exactly the

mocked step still fails and the debugger lands on it immediately.

Add Render Blueprint for a persistent, single-instance host

Vercel's serverless model can route requests to different Lambda

VIZU_DEMO_MODE=1 pre-set, matching what DEPLOY.md already recommended
but never gave a concrete, no-spend path for.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Confine artifact and hashFiles filesystem access to the workspace

Both paths run regardless of VIZU_DEMO_MODE - only `run:` steps are gated
by isSimulationOnly(), so `uses:` handlers and the expression evaluator
were reachable on the public demo, on a single shared process.

Artifact handlers: `with: path:` and `with: name:` went into path.join()
unchecked, so `../` or an absolute value escaped both the job workspace
(read) and the artifact store (write). Paths now resolve through a
confinement helper that rejects anything landing outside its base, and
escaping glob patterns are refused outright with an explanatory note
rather than silently skipped. A shared link replays `uses:` steps on
page load, so this was reachable with one click and no further input.

hashFiles(): unrestricted globs plus uncapped synchronous reads. Now
rejects absolute/`..` patterns and reports when a match set exceeds the
file-count or byte limit - reported rather than truncated, since a
silently partial hash is wrong in a way callers cannot detect.

The session-less playground passed process.cwd() as the evaluation
workspace, which let an anonymous caller use hashFiles() as an existence
oracle over the server's own files; it now gets a dedicated empty dir.

Also stops following symlinks out of either tree, and caps artifact copy
loops, which are synchronous on the process serving every visitor.

Verified against a local production server in demo mode: traversal and
absolute paths rejected on both surfaces, an off-workspace canary file
untouched, ordinary relative paths still working. 433 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Bound matrix expansion and mask secrets in expression errors

Matrix expansion was an unbounded Cartesian product built synchronously
before the response: ten axes of ten values is ten billion combinations
from a few lines of YAML, and the workflow-length limit does not bound it
because a matrix multiplies. On one shared persistent process that hangs
the instance for every visitor, not just the caller.

Combination counts now come from the axis lengths without building
anything, and createSession refuses an oversized workflow before
allocating any lane or step record - the limit per job matrix is 256,
which is the ceiling GitHub itself enforces, plus totals across jobs so
individually-legal matrices cannot add up to the same problem. The route
maps the refusal to 400 and removes the scratch workspace it had already
created, never a real working tree the user pointed the debugger at.

Secret masking: the expression-evaluate route masked `result` and `trace`
but returned `error` verbatim, and fromJSON() quotes the text it failed
to parse - so fromJSON(secrets.TOKEN) handed the secret straight back.
The same applied to a step's `ifError` and to the engine errors raised by
a failed `run:` interpolation or spawn, which also reach the explanation
prompt sent to the Anthropic API. Masked at the record level so both the
client-visible field and the outbound prompt are covered.

Verified against a local production server: the ten-billion matrix is
refused in 29ms with no leftover workspace, a 256-combination matrix
still expands, and fromJSON(secrets.TOKEN) now reports `invalid JSON:
***`. 445 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Apply GitHub's default success() check to explicit if: conditions

Writing an `if:` does not opt out of the implicit "everything before this
succeeded" gate - only naming a status function does. GitHub documents
this as "a default status check of success() is applied unless you
include one of these functions", and it is why `if: always()` is needed
to upload artifacts after a failure rather than any truthy condition.

The engine only applied the gate when `if:` was absent, so a step with
`if: true` ran after an earlier step failed, and a job with `if: true`
became ready after a failed or skipped dependency. For a tool whose whole
claim is showing what GitHub would do without pushing, running a step
GitHub would skip is the worst direction to be wrong in: there is no
reference to compare against, so the user has no way to notice.

Detection is syntactic on the parsed expression, so `success()` inside a
string literal doesn't count as opting out, and `!cancelled()` does.
When the gate suppresses a condition that evaluated true, the existing
if-warning field explains why - the surprise is the whole point of
showing it. That advice names ${{ !cancelled() }} with its wrapper,
because a bare leading `!` is a YAML tag and won't parse.

This is a behavior change to the execution engine, not a security fix,
and it is one an earlier review of mine wrongly dismissed as correct.

Verified in a browser: after a failed step, `if: true` shows
"if: true -> false" with the explanation and a skipped marker, while
`if: always()` runs. 457 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Resolve confinement through the filesystem, not just the path string

A follow-up review reproduced four escapes past the previous commit, all
of the same shape: path.resolve() compares text, so a symlink inside the
workspace pointing out of it passes the check and the caller then reads
or writes the real target. Confirmed all four locally before fixing -
hashFiles through a symlinked directory (literal path and glob), an
artifact whose root is a symlink, and a download destination that is one.

Confinement now resolves both the base and the target through the
filesystem, handling paths that don't exist yet by resolving the deepest
existing ancestor and re-appending the missing tail, and returns the real
path so callers operate on that rather than the symlinked route. Shared
by the artifact handlers and hashFiles, which had near-duplicate checks.

A NUL byte gets its own rejection: fs throws a TypeError rather than a
not-found on one, which the ancestor walk would otherwise read as "does
not exist yet" and let through. It is reachable straight from pasted
YAML, where \0 is an ordinary escape.

The playground's empty scratch directory is replaced by removing the
capability: hashFiles now refuses when there is no session rather than
reading any directory, and the process.cwd() fallbacks behind it are
gone, so no context can reach the server's own tree by omitting a cwd.

Separately, an exception anywhere in a step left lane.status at
"running", which nothing resets - every later control call then rejected
the lane as already running and the session was wedged for good. Steps
now record an unexpected throw as a visible engine error and stay
steppable, with a last-resort reset in both control entry points.

Caps are now true bounds, refusing a file that would exceed them rather
than stopping once already over, and artifact copying has a byte cap
alongside the file count.

481 tests pass, including the four reproductions as regression tests,
symlink cases on both ends, the byte limits, and the wedged-lane
recovery.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Add address and instance-wide abuse limits; fix two limit/masking edges

Abuse limits: the owner id is a cookie the visitor controls, so clearing
it bought a fresh allowance and the per-owner limit bounded nobody. Two
more scopes now sit alongside it - per client address, deliberately
looser since a NAT shares one, and a global ceiling that bounds the
shared instance however many identities the traffic is spread across,
plus a cap on total live sessions. The address comes from the last
x-forwarded-for entry: a client can prepend entries but not the one the
proxy appends. Capacity is checked across all scopes before any records
a hit, so a request refused by one doesn't spend another's budget.

Bucket eviction: the map kept one entry per owner id ever seen and never
dropped any, which on a long-running single process grows without bound.
Entries with nothing left inside the window are now swept, at most once
per window so the cost is proportional to the map rather than to each
request.

Two edge cases found in review, both reproduced first:

fromJSON() truncated its input to 60 characters before building the
error, and masking searches for each secret's full text - so a secret
longer than the cutoff left an unmatchable prefix and printed most of
itself back. A short secret passed the existing test while a long one
leaked. The value is no longer quoted at all; the length is enough to
tell an empty value from a malformed one.

The matrix limit counted one lane per include entry, but an include
usually merges into combos that already exist and adds no row, so a
legitimate 256-combination matrix with one merging include was rejected
as 257. The pre-allocation guard now measures only the cross product -
the part that grows exponentially - and the real total is checked after
expansion, which is safe once the product is known to be bounded.

Also corrects the skip warning's wording: failure() runs a step only
when something failed, it does not run it "regardless".

494 tests pass, including the long-secret leak, the 256-plus-include
matrix, cookie-reset abuse, and bucket eviction as regression cases.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011SE3csbYNdw3sSMFV4LSyN

Mask secrets across output chunk boundaries; fix first-upload regression

Cross-chunk masking: each captured chunk was masked on its own, so a
secret written in two calls left one half in each and matched neither.
The redacted stdout read `***` while the interleaved view still showed
the whole token once its chunks were read end to end. Redaction is now
computed over the concatenation and re-split on the original boundaries,
which also covers a secret straddling a stdout/stderr switch; the mask is
emitted where the secret begins and dropped from the chunks it continues
into. Reproduced end to end first - two printf calls either side of a
sleep - and the same script now yields `***`.

This also adds the first unit tests for the masking module, which had
none. That absence is why a bug in it survived: every existing test
exercised masking only through a caller that happened to pass whole
strings.

First-upload regression, introduced by the confinement commit: the
artifact store is the confinement base, a base has to exist to be
resolved, and the engine creates that store lazily - so the first upload
of any session was refused, reporting an escaping artifact name. Every
existing test pre-created the store in its fixture, which hid it

separately as well as interleaved, and the redactions from all three are
unioned onto the chunks - so a split within one stream, a split across a

Snapshot each step's environment instead of recomputing it

The context view of an already-executed step was built from the present:
`resolveEffectiveEnv` composed the workflow and job layers with whatever
`$GITHUB_ENV` and What-If held *now*. So a later step writing COLOR=blue
made the first step appear to have seen blue, and a What-If override to
green made every step appear to have seen green. Worse than a wrong
value - a debugger showing a past that never happened, with nothing to
compare against.

Each step now records what it was actually given, at the moment it ran:

- envBefore: the environment supplied to that step, its own `env:`
  layer included, captured before the `if:` is evaluated so a skipped
  step still shows what it would have had.
- envAfter: `$GITHUB_ENV` as it stood when the step finished - what the
  steps after it inherit.

The context route serves the snapshot for any step behind the pointer.
The step *at* the pointer keeps recomputing, because it has not run yet:
there the live answer is the right one, since it is what running it now
would use.

Snapshots are kept raw, like Lane.env, and stripped from the serialized
session entirely rather than masked - the context endpoint serves the one
step being inspected, so the payload does not need an env map per step
per lane, and there is one fewer copy to redact.

reaching the client. Verified over HTTP: after overriding to green, step

expression won't evaluate. The context is assembled with a provisional

needs the rest of the context.

Bound anonymous expression evaluation

`format()` amplifies: a placeholder may be repeated as often as the format
string likes, so `format('{0}{0}{0}{0}', x)` quadruples its input while
writing it once, and nesting that multiplies. A 339-character expression
produced a 268MB string - reachable with no session, so session-creation
limits never saw it. At 40 levels the same trick reaches gigabytes.

Three bounds, because no single one is enough:

Every value an expression function produces is now capped at 100,000
characters, checked *as* the value is built rather than on the finished
string - a format string may repeat one placeholder any number of times, so
the overshoot happens inside the loop. Capping each produced value bounds the
whole evaluation, since every nesting level has to materialise its own result
before the level above can use it: the innermost call that would exceed the
cap fails and nothing larger is allocated.

The response has its own shared character budget. Per-string caps alone were
not enough, because a trace carries a value and a source label per node and
the node count grows with the input too: a maximal 7.9KB expression still
answered with ~1MB. Strings are capped individually and the trace stops being
walked once the total is spent, with the node saying it was truncated rather
than appearing childless. All of it runs strictly after masking - truncating
first and masking the remainder is the leak this codebase keeps finding.

The endpoint now has its own rate-limit allowance, in a bucket namespaced per
action so playground traffic can never be what stops a visitor opening a
session. `checkCreateLimit` became a thin wrapper over a general
`checkLimit`.

Also fixes the 500 on a non-string `expression`: `.trim()` ran before the
type check, so a malformed request was answered as a server failure. It is a
400 now, alongside a length cap on the expression text - parsing is recursive
descent, so unbounded input is also unbounded nesting depth.

Verified over HTTP against a production build: the 339-character amplifier is
refused, a maximal-nesting 7.9KB request answers in 126KB instead of ~1MB,
`{"expression":42}` returns 400, and the 601st evaluation returns 429 while
session creation from the same visitor still succeeds.

569 tests pass; typecheck, lint and build clean.
